clinicalPearls: Presents as grouped erythematous papules, papulopustules and fine scaling around the mouth with characteristic sparing of a narrow zone immediately adjacent to the vermilion border.
Predominantly affects young women, and also occurs in children as periorificial dermatitis around the mouth, nose and eyes.
Strongly associated with topical corticosteroid use on the face, and also with inhaled and intranasal corticosteroids.
A rebound flare on withdrawal of topical steroids is characteristic and should be anticipated and explained to the patient.
First-line management is 'zero therapy' — stopping all topical corticosteroids, heavy cosmetics and occlusive skin care.
Oral tetracyclines are effective in adults, while macrolides are preferred in young children and pregnancy where tetracyclines are contraindicated.
A granulomatous variant occurs particularly in children and shows non-caseating granulomas on histology.
Fluorinated toothpaste, occlusive cosmetics and Demodex have been implicated as contributory factors.
reference.pathophysiology: Perioral dermatitis is a multifactorial follicular and epidermal barrier disorder rather than a true eczema. Impairment of the epidermal barrier and a follicular inflammatory reaction are provoked or aggravated by topical, inhaled or intranasal corticosteroids, occlusive cosmetics and skin care products, and fluorinated dental products. Follicular micro-organisms including Demodex mites and fusobacteria have been implicated in perpetuating the inflammation, and the periorificial distribution reflects the involvement of facial pilosebaceous units.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on morphology and distribution in most cases
Detailed history of topical, inhaled and intranasal corticosteroid and cosmetic exposure
Skin swab if secondary bacterial infection or marked pustulation is suspected
Patch testing when allergic contact dermatitis is a differential
Skin biopsy in atypical or granulomatous presentations
Skin scraping or examination for Demodex in refractory cases
redFlags: Ocular involvement with blepharitis or conjunctivitis requiring ophthalmology assessment
Failure to respond to appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Granulomatous features raising the possibility of cutaneous sarcoidosis
Progressive facial swelling or systemic symptoms
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is good, with resolution over weeks to a few months once corticosteroids are withdrawn and antibiotic therapy is given, although relapse can occur if provoking factors are reintroduced.
pitfalls: Treating with topical corticosteroids, which briefly improve then worsen the eruption and cause rebound flares.
Misdiagnosing the condition as acne and missing the steroid or cosmetic trigger.
Overlooking inhaled or intranasal corticosteroids as an ongoing source.
Not warning the patient about the expected rebound flare on steroid cessation, leading to loss of adherence.
management: Institute 'zero therapy' first by stopping all topical corticosteroids and heavy occlusive cosmetics and skin-care products
Anticipate and explain the characteristic rebound flare on withdrawal of topical corticosteroids and manage it supportively
Prescribe a topical anti-inflammatory agent such as metronidazole, azelaic acid or a topical calcineurin inhibitor
Give an oral tetracycline for moderate, severe or refractory disease in adults
Use a macrolide instead in young children and in pregnancy, where tetracyclines are contraindicated
Advise gentle skin care and avoidance of fluorinated dental products and provoking factors to reduce relapse
Consider treatment directed at Demodex in refractory cases
